strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: characterizing the invariance manifold of visual units goes beyond MEIs and predefined transformations, addressing a real gap in feature visualization and neuroscience methodology.

The bi-objective (stretch/squeeze) formulation is elegant and unifying, recovering both invariance search and adversarial example synthesis as special cases, with a principled Pareto-front-based multi-objective treatment.

Unusually thorough and careful evaluation: activation regimes benchmarked against natural image statistics (Fig. S1), representational distance analysis with sensible control metrics, PCA+SVC separability, and a well-designed human 12-AFC psychophysics experiment (n=25) with GLMM statistics, BH-corrected contrasts, screening, and IRB/compensation details.

Subsampling experiments (Section D) directly address the key practical obstacle (sparse neural recordings) for translating the method to biological systems, and hidden-layer experiments (Section C) demonstrate generality beyond category-selective readout units.
Good transparency: pseudocode, hyperparameters, hardware, early-stopping criteria, open source code and data; a thoughtful discussion of limitations and future directions.

Interesting empirical findings, e.g., opposing recognizability trends as a function of stretching depth for robust vs. standard networks, and the capacity-dependent behavior of standard observer models.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the method is essentially XDREAM-style evolutionary optimization (same generative model, CMA-ES) with modified objectives. The core contribution is a re-framing rather than a new algorithmic capability, and prior work (e.g., Cadena et al. on diverse visualizations; Wang & Ponce tuning landscapes) already edges toward invariance probing.

Missing direct comparison to the closest competing approach, model metamers (Feather et al. 2023), which is the dominant gradient-based way to probe invariance landscapes. Claims that SnS explores invariance 'more precisely' than alternatives would be far better supported with a head-to-head quantitative comparison rather than only affine augmentation baselines.

Findings are largely confirmatory of prior literature: robust networks produce more human-interpretable invariant/metamer images echoes Feather et al., and the adversarial examples mirror known results (Gaziv et al., Engstrom et al.). The capacity-dependent observer results are novel but not fully explained.

The generator prior (fc7 model from Dosovitskiy & Brox) necessarily constrains the space of discoverable invariances; the paper does not quantify how much of the observed 'invariance landscape' reflects the network's true tolerances versus the generative prior's biases. This is acknowledged implicitly but not analyzed.

Scope limited to two ResNet-50 instances; no ViTs or other architectures despite discussion of inductive biases, and no actual biological validation (only simulated subsampling), so the neuroscience significance remains prospective.

Mean activation 'reduction of 111%' for adversarial examples is a poorly defined statistic (suppression exceeding 100% of MEI activation, possibly going negative); some quantitative reporting (e.g., effect of the ad hoc Pareto selection strategies) lacks ablation.

Some notation/typos (e.g., 'Optmization', L_squeeze defined as maximizing euclidean distance in Eq. 1 wording, 'Layer4_conv7' vs 'layer4_conv7' inconsistency), and the invariance experiments in Section 4.2 use robust networks' MEIs as references while Section 4.3 uses natural images, complicating comparability.

strengths: The unified bi-objective (stretch/squeeze) formulation elegantly connects invariance and adversarial sensitivity as duals of the same optimization problem, which is conceptually appealing.

The experimental pipeline is thorough: gradient-free CMA-ES optimization with Pareto fronts, proper early-stopping criteria, convergence statistics (Suppl. A.3), and openly released code and data support reproducibility.
The human psychophysics experiment is well executed, with IRB approval, screening, appropriate compensation, GLMM-based statistics with FDR correction, and replication across multiple observer CNNs.
The subsampling analysis (Suppl. Section D) is a genuinely useful addition, addressing a critical constraint (sparse neural recordings) for real neuroscience applications.
The hierarchical representational distance analysis (Fig. 4) provides quantitative support for the qualitative claim of layer-specific invariance axes.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core method is essentially XDREAM-style evolutionary optimization (already applied to artificial networks in [6, 30, 31]) repurposed with an invariance/adversarial objective. The claim of being 'the first gradientless approach to systematically infer invariance manifolds' is overstated; the qualitative conclusions (robust networks yield more human-interpretable images) largely re-confirm Feather et al. [15] with a different synthesis method.

A serious uncontrolled confound: all discovered 'invariances' are constrained by the fixed generative prior (Dosovitskiy-Brox fc7 generator). Differences between low/mid/high-level invariances, and between standard vs. robust networks, may partly reflect what the generator can and cannot express, rather than the units' true invariance manifolds. No experiment disentangles this (e.g., varying generators, or unconstrained pixel optimization as a control).

Narrow evaluation scope: only ResNet-50 (two training variants) as subject network, only 77 readout units plus a small hidden-layer sample, and no comparison against gradient-based invariance/metamer methods, which are feasible for CNNs. The generality claims ('model-agnostic framework') are not supported by experiments on any other architecture (e.g., ViTs), which the authors themselves concede in the limitations.

The 'invariance' achieved is questionable: invariant images show a 34% ± 11% reduction in target activation, a substantial drop from the MEI reference, so these stimuli are only partially invariant. Additionally, the reported '111% ± 7%' activation reduction for adversarial examples exceeds 100%, suggesting normalization issues or an error that is not explained.

Several analyses are weak or close to tautological: the SVC/PCA separability result (Fig. 3c) largely confirms that images optimized in different spaces look different — an expected outcome; layer-wise L2 distances across layers of vastly different dimensionality are compared without discussion of comparability.

The Pareto front selection strategies (exploitative vs. uniform) are introduced ad hoc without justification or ablation, weakening the claimed 'unbiased' nature of the method. Sensitivity to this choice, population size, and iteration budget is not assessed.

The finding that large standard observer networks classify standard-network invariant images well is left essentially unexplained, and the ecological significance of the 12-AFC results for understanding vision is unclear.

Overall, the paper reads as a competent but incremental application of existing optimization machinery to a benchmark CNN, with headline conclusions already established in prior work; the contribution is not competitive for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper introduces Stretch-and-Squeeze (SnS), a unified bi-objective optimization framework that recasts invariance probing and adversarial example synthesis as dual formulations of the same problem. This is a clean, well-motivated conceptual contribution that goes beyond predefined transformations (affine) and strict representational identity (metamers).

The method is genuinely model-agnostic and gradient-free (CMA-ES + generative prior), which positions it well for neuroscience applications where differentiable digital twins are unavailable. The demonstration that results hold under heavy subsampling of the representation space (Supplementary Section D) directly addresses a key experimental constraint and strengthens the claimed relevance to in vivo work.

Evaluation is comprehensive: quantitative convergence statistics against natural-image activation distributions (Fig. S1), SVC-based separability of invariant image classes, representational distance analysis with sensible control baselines (reference variability, within/between-category distances), and a well-designed human psychophysics experiment (25 participants, 12-AFC, GLMM with appropriate random effects, Benjamini-Hochberg correction) plus cross-observer validation with multiple CNNs.

The comparison of invariant images between standard and robustly trained ResNet-50 extends Feather et al.'s metamer findings in an informative way, and the reported dissociation between small and large standard observer networks is an interesting, non-obvious empirical observation.
Good reproducibility posture: pseudocode, hyperparameters, hardware specification, and public code/data availability are provided.
weaknesses: Generality is limited: all main results are based on a single architecture (ResNet-50, only two instances - standard and one L2-robust variant). The authors themselves acknowledge that extension to other architectures (e.g., ViTs) is future work, but for a method paper claiming to characterize 'invariance landscapes' this is a meaningful scope restriction.

Novelty is moderate rather than groundbreaking. The core machinery (evolutionary optimization over latent codes of a generative model, à la XDREAM) is adapted from prior work [10, 30]; the main novelty lies in the bi-objective/Pareto-front formulation and the systematic layer-wise application. The headline findings (robust networks yield more human-interpretable invariances) largely replicate directions already established by metamers work [15, 18].

A potential confound is underexplored: the discovered 'invariances' are necessarily filtered through the generative model's prior. The paper notes the generator regularizes toward natural statistics, but does not quantify how much of the observed layer-specific invariance structure reflects the subject network versus the generator's own invariance manifold. A control using a different generator, or comparison against gradient-based metamer optimization, would substantially strengthen the claims.

The stretch/squeeze objectives rely on Euclidean distance in raw activation space, which may be dominated by uninformative directions at higher layers; no analysis of whether the results are robust to the choice of distance metric (e.g., normalized or representational-similarity-based distances) is provided.

Computational cost of the evolutionary approach (500 iterations, population 50, per unit per seed) is reported only implicitly; a cost/effectiveness comparison with gradient-based alternatives is missing, and the discussion of why gradient-free is preferable when the networks are in fact differentiable (all experiments are on CNNs) is thin.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., the interpretation of the opposite recognizability trends across stretching depth, and the capacity/robustness explanation for large standard observers, are speculative and not directly tested. The classification of invariant images as 'luminance/contrast', 'texture', 'pose' is largely qualitative with SVC pixel-space discrimination serving as only indirect corroboration.

Minor issues: reference [50] is an anonymous self-citation with a broken URL; several figures have low legibility of axis labels; the adversarial 'attack' results are restricted to a narrow configuration and are not benchmarked against standard attack methods (e.g., PGD under matched pixel budgets).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated methodological contribution: SnS is, to the authors' knowledge, the first gradient-free, model-agnostic framework for systematically characterizing invariance manifolds of visual units, unifying invariance and adversarial searches under a single bi-objective (Pareto) formulation built on CMA-ES. This fills a genuine gap between gradient-based approaches (metamers, MEIs, CPPN-based methods) and gradient-free MEI search (XDREAM).

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: the method is validated on multiple architectures (ResNet50/18, VGG16_bn, ViTs, both standard and L2/L∞-robust), multiple stretching levels, readout and hidden-layer units, with careful quantitative controls (convergence analysis, single-loss ablations demonstrating the necessity of the dual objective, subsampling robustness for neuroscience applicability, representational distance analyses, intrinsic dimension estimation).

Strong empirical centerpiece: the human psychophysics experiment (12-AFC, n=25, GLMM with proper multiple-comparison correction) combined with observer-network experiments reveals a genuinely new finding - opposite interpretability trends for robust vs. standard networks as a function of stretching depth - which is complementary to and clearly distinguished from the metamer results of Feather et al. (2023), with an explicit quantitative comparison (Tables S3, S4).

Good positioning and honest discussion of related work, including explicit clarification of how SnS relates to metamers (which emerge as a special case of the squeeze-only objective), and clear articulation of limitations and future in vivo applications.
Good reproducibility: detailed pseudocode, hyperparameters, hardware description, open source code and data, and a thorough supplementary with statistical procedures.
weaknesses: No direct biological validation: despite being motivated primarily by neuroscience, the in vivo claims rest on simulated subsampling of CNN representations; the neural signal variability, noise, and closed-loop constraints of real experiments are only discussed, not tested.

The generative prior (Dosovitskiy & Brox fc7 generator) is a potential confound: the discovered invariance manifolds are necessarily constrained to the generator's output space, and the paper acknowledges (but does not quantify) how this prior shapes the found transformations; comparisons to gradient-based metamers are thus not fully controlled for the search-space difference.

Some headline conclusions (robust networks produce more human-interpretable invariances; adversarial training sculpts representations toward human-aligned features) largely confirm prior work (Feather et al., 2023; Gaziv et al., 2023); the truly novel part is the depth-dependent divergence, which is demonstrated for a relatively limited set of reference images (12 categories) in the behavioral experiment.

Gradient-free optimization is computationally expensive relative to gradient-based alternatives (500 iterations x population 50 per run, thousands of runs), and the paper does not provide a head-to-head efficiency comparison or explore whether the same objectives could be optimized with gradients where available, leaving the practical advantage in artificial-network settings (where gradients do exist) underexplored.

The scope of the mechanistic interpretation is somewhat qualitative: the semantic labels of invariances (luminance/texture/pose) are inferred from visual inspection plus a PCA/SVC separability analysis, without a stronger quantitative taxonomy linking stretching layers to specific transformation types.

strengths: The proposed Stretch-and-Squeeze (SnS) framework is well-motivated: probing invariance manifolds rather than only MEIs addresses a genuine gap in feature visualization, and the bi-objective (stretch/squeeze) formulation that unifies invariant and adversarial synthesis is elegant and clearly formalized (Pareto-based, gradient-free, model-agnostic).

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this kind of paper: 77 readout units with 10 seeds per condition, convergence and single-loss ablation experiments, control distance metrics (within/between-category, MEI variability), an SVM-based separability analysis, intrinsic-dimension estimates, subsampling robustness tests, L2 and L∞ robust networks, ViTs, and a systematic comparison against metamers (Tables S3, S4).

The human psychophysics experiment (25 participants, 12-AFC, GLMM with FDR-corrected planned contrasts) plus a large panel of observer networks provides a solid empirical basis for the main finding: opposite depth-dependence of interpretability for robust vs. standard networks, which extends and nuances Feather et al. (2023) in an interesting way.
Reproducibility is addressed with pseudocode, hyperparameters, hardware details, released code and data, and an IRB-approved, well-documented human experiment.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The method is essentially XDREAM (Xiao & Kreiman, 2020) with a second objective term added; the authors themselves frame SnS as 'building upon an existing framework for finding MEIs'. The Pareto-based bi-objective CMA-ES search is a competent but not conceptually deep extension, and metamer synthesis is shown to be a special case of the squeeze term, further narrowing the technical delta.

The central claim of neuroscientific applicability is not validated. All experiments are on artificial networks; the 'sparse recording' argument is a simulation of subsampling synthetic activations, which does not address the real bottlenecks of in vivo work (neural noise, trial-by-trial variability, limited recording time, non-stationarity) beyond a paragraph of future-work discussion. The paper's strongest selling point — gradient-free probing of biological vision — remains speculative.

A significant confound is unaddressed: results depend heavily on the Dosovitskiy & Brox (2016) generator prior. The authors acknowledge that strong generative priors regularize the search, but the extent to which the discovered 'invariance manifolds' reflect unit properties vs. the generator's latent structure is not quantified. No comparison with alternative generators (e.g., diffusion or GANs) is attempted, despite acknowledging them in limitations.

Interpretability is measured only via 12-way classification accuracy of a small set (12 categories, 10 references), a narrow proxy for 'human-alignment of invariances'; the headline claim that 'L2 adversarial training fails to increase the interpretability of high-level invariances' rests on this restricted paradigm and on readout-unit targets that encode whole classes, not on units more analogous to neurons.

Quantitative depth comparisons are largely relegated to qualitative descriptions ('luminance/contrast vs. texture vs. pose') with only an SVC-on-PCA separability analysis; several key analyses (ID estimation on a single example unit, L∞ results, ViT results) are one-off demonstrations rather than systematic evaluations, weakening the generality of the hierarchical claims.

Positioning against concurrent/related gradient-free invariance work (e.g., Wang & Ponce 2022b 'Tuning landscapes') is thin; the claim to be 'the first gradientless approach to systematically infer invariance manifolds' is stated but not rigorously differentiated from that line of work.

The computational cost of CMA-ES in a 4096-d code space (quadratic scaling acknowledged) is non-trivial, and no comparison is given to simpler gradient-based bi-objective alternatives in the cases where gradients are available — leaving open whether the gradient-free constraint is worth its cost outside neuroscience, where the method is admittedly a poor fit.

strengths: Novel, well-motivated methodological contribution: SnS is, to the authors' knowledge, the first systematic gradient-free framework for probing invariance manifolds of visual units, unifying invariance search and adversarial synthesis in a single Pareto-based bi-objective formulation. This is a genuine gap relative to gradient-based metamers/MEI work.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: validation of adversarial and invariant image generation against affine transformations (Fig. 2), single-loss ablations showing the dual loss is necessary (Suppl. D), convergence analysis against natural-image activation regimes (Fig. S2, Table S1), representational distance analysis with proper within/between-category controls (Fig. S3), and comparison to metamer synthesis showing methodological complementarity (Tables S3-S4).

Strong empirical finding with broad scope: the opposite interpretability trends between L2-robust and standard networks as a function of stretching depth (Fig. 4c, e), replicated across multiple architectures (ResNet18, VGG16_bn, ViT) and extended to L∞ robustification (Fig. S11), meaningfully extends Feather et al. (2023) and provides a more granular picture of model-human misalignment.

Human behavioral validation with appropriate statistical rigor: 25 participants in a 12-AFC task, GLMM with random intercepts, omnibus test plus planned contrasts with Benjamini-Hochberg correction (Table S2), and ethically transparent reporting (IRB, compensation details, photosensitivity warnings).

Good neuroscientific relevance and thoroughness: subsampling analysis (Section F) directly addresses the sparse-recording constraint of in vivo experiments; the discussion of closed-loop adaptation is realistic. Code, pseudocode, hyperparameters, hardware, and data availability statements are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Moderate methodological novelty: the core algorithm is a relatively straightforward re-purposing of the XDREAM/CMA-ES machinery with a two-objective fitness function and Pareto-front sorting. The conceptual contribution is real but incremental, and much of the headline finding (robust networks produce more human-interpretable invariances) re-confirms prior metamers work (Feather et al., 2023) with a new twist.

The fixed generator prior (Dosovitskiy & Brox 2016, fc7, n=4096) is a significant confound: all discovered invariances are bounded by what this low-capacity, dated generator can express, and the interpretability of the images may partly reflect the generator's statistics rather than the subject network's invariances. The paper acknowledges this in the limitations but does not quantify the generator's contribution (e.g., no control using the generator with a matched random objective, no comparison with a second generative model).

Lack of biological validation despite strong neuroscientific claims: all 'neuroscience applicability' evidence is simulated (subsampled CNN layers). The in vivo applicability, and hence a substantial part of the paper's stated significance, remains untested; claims should be tempered accordingly.

Qualitative characterizations of layer-specific invariances (luminance/contrast, texture, pose) rest partly on informal semantic labels; the PCA+SVC separability analysis (Fig. 3c) shows the image sets are discriminable in pixel space but does not directly validate the semantic interpretation of the transformation axes.

Scalability and completeness concerns: results are largely anchored on 77 readout units of one model for the main analysis, 12 ImageNet categories and 25 human participants for the behavioral study, and ID/geometry analysis on a single example unit; CMA-ES in a 4096-d space is also computationally heavy relative to gradient-based alternatives, which could limit adoption.

Some claims are slightly stronger than the evidence: e.g., characterizing SnS as revealing 'the actual axes of image variation a unit learned to tolerate' assumes the Pareto-optimal solutions span the invariant manifold, but the exploration may be biased by initialization and generator prior; the ID analysis (Section H) is on one unit and cannot support general geometric conclusions.
